headline: Navi Pillay, 85, wins the Nobel Peace Prize
summary: Navi Pillay, 85, a bus driver's daughter from Durban, judged the Rwanda genocide tribunal and ran UN human rights. The Nobel committee says her work got war crimes prosecuted. Israel called the award a "grotesque weaponisation". Hours later the US sanctioned the International Criminal Court. Trump told a rally he had "never heard" of her.

cover_question.q: Why would a judge win a peace prize?

cover_answer: Her courts tried the people who ran wars. That counts.
table_question: Can a referee be fair if one team keeps booing her?

5-7.script: A judge named Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize yesterday. She is 85, and her dad drove a bus in South Africa. She grew up to be a judge for the whole world, like a referee for countries. When she heard, she said it must be a joke. It wasn't, and today is a good day.
5-7.why: One person, one dad with a bus, one referee. A seven-year-old can hold that.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old reasons from what is in front of them and takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script hands over one person, a dad who drove a bus, and one picture for the work: a referee for countries. Genocide and courts stay out. Expect "what did the bad people do?" Hurt a lot of people in a war, and she was the judge.

8-12.script: Navi Pillay grew up a bus driver's daughter under apartheid. First non-white woman on South Africa's high court, then a Rwanda genocide judge, then the UN's rights chief. The committee says that got war crimes prosecuted. A referee who writes the fouls down after the game.
8-12.why: A ladder of firsts, each a bigger court.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out whether rules apply to everyone, and who gets to apply them. So the script climbs her career court by court: a province, a country, a tribunal, the UN. The referee writing fouls down after the game is the mechanism they know. Expect "who makes countries obey?" Nobody. The prize says the trials matter anyway.

13-17.script: Can a court work when the powerful ignore it? Navi Pillay won the Peace Prize for getting war crimes prosecuted. The same day, the US sanctioned the ICC, where she once sat. Second: Israel calls her Gaza inquiry a lie. Can a prize for law stay neutral?
13-17.why: Law as necessity, law as weapon. Let them hold both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once, and this one demands it: law as "an absolute necessity", the committee's words, and the award as a weapon, Israel's. The script gives both and asks if a prize for law can stay neutral. Expect "who is right about Gaza?" Her inquiry's finding, Israel's rejection, the committee's no position.

5-7.a: A gold medal for someone who helped stop fighting or made the world fairer. She got it for being a fair judge.

8-12.q: Why would a judge win a peace prize?
8-12.a: Wars stay ended when those who ran them face a court. That was her job.

8-12.q: Why is Trump mad about it?
8-12.a: He wants it himself. He said he'd never heard of her.

13-17.q: Can a court work with no army behind it?
13-17.a: The committee says it has to. The US sanctioned the ICC the same day.
Her UN inquiry said Israel committed genocidal acts in Gaza. Israel rejects that.

Her courts tried the people who ran wars. That counts.

Navi Pillay, 85, a bus driver's daughter from Durban, judged the Rwanda genocide tribunal and ran UN human rights. The Nobel committee says her work got war crimes prosecuted.
